Replay

Self-contained save bundles

3 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓

A bundle combines an opaque checkpoint/root document with the exact asset payloads it requires. The root remains independently encoded; assets are sorted by reference and deduplicated. Capturing gameplay state does not silently capture an entire cache.

bundle_encode(root, refs, cache, meta) validates references, availability and total size before allocating the output. Missing content fails before any file write. The format permits a 1 MiB root, 32 assets and a 16 MiB total file. A small canonical header stores version, lengths, asset count and the body's SHA-256; the appended body contains the root followed by canonical references and payloads. This supports files larger than the network envelope limit without weakening that limit.

bundle_decode checks the header, exact lengths, body digest, sorted/unique references and each asset's content ID. It returns read-only views into the supplied file bytes and changes no cache. Keep those bytes alive until the views are no longer used. bundle_install checks every asset, optional format validators and aggregate cache capacity before installing anything. Invalid data, validation failure or capacity exhaustion preserves existing entries and pins.

The Godot helpers checkpoint_bundle_write and checkpoint_bundle_read connect the format to the existing checkpoint codec and staged file writer. Read returns owned file bytes plus a borrowed view; the caller must check identity/authority policy and dependency completeness before installing assets and resuming. Outer and inner content/epoch/tick metadata must agree. Callbacks, reconnect credentials and live transport objects remain outside the archive.

checkpoint_bundle_encode returns owned bundle bytes without performing I/O. checkpoint_bundle_decode validates supplied bytes and returns a borrowed view. Both share the same checkpoint/metadata validation with the file helpers. This lets an asynchronous backend store one complete bundle and report its own commit receipt. Scrapyard uses these helpers with IndexedDB for browser solo saves.

Plain checkpoint files are also readable, with an empty asset set. A game that requires external assets must reject such a file unless those dependencies are actually included by an explicitly supported alternate mechanism. Scrapyard checks every player's image reference and requires it to be in the bundle, even if an unrelated local cache happens to contain the same image.

The writer encodes everything before opening the staging file and then uses the existing flush/close/rename path. This is a process-crash boundary, not a portable power-loss guarantee. One writer owns a save path. The format does not grant a coordinator lease or authorize loading another player's local seat.

bundle_replace_root(original, new_root, content) supports explicit application upgrades. It validates the entire original bundle, preserves its metadata and asset records/payloads, and returns owned bytes with new lengths and a new body digest. The source is unchanged. The replacement root must be 1 byte–1 MiB and the complete output must remain within 16 MiB. This generic operation does not validate the replacement root's semantics, metadata or dependency completeness; the application must do that before publication. See the protocol-6 checkpoint bridge.

The optional target_content argument explicitly updates the outer content ID for an application-schema conversion. Zero (the default) preserves the source content. The source is always validated against the required content argument first. Epoch and tick remain unchanged. The caller must validate that the converted root actually declares the new content before writing or restoring the bundle.
